question: Six health links found by comparing groups of people. Which turned out to be cause and effect, and which fell apart?
answer: A link survives when its obvious rival is ruled out. Breastfeeding mothers, sunbathers and vitamin takers differ from other people in ways that matter; compare like with like and the link vanishes or flips. Smoking, HPV and lead passed the harder tests: more exposure, more harm, and less harm once it was removed.
move: Before believing a link, ask how the people in it came to be there.
ask: Which habit do I credit for my health that people like me simply tend to have?

items.note: Smokers get far more lung cancer.
items.verdict: No trial ever made people smoke. Dose, timing and quitting proved it anyway.

items.note: Breastfed children score higher on IQ tests.
items.verdict: Compared with their own siblings, the gap vanished. The mothers explained it.

items.note: In some surveys, users get more melanoma.
items.verdict: Sunbathers use more of it. In a trial, daily use halved new melanomas.

items.note: Women with this virus get cervical cancer.
items.verdict: Where girls were vaccinated against it, the cancer has almost vanished among them.

items.note: People taking it had fewer heart attacks.
items.verdict: Takers were healthier to start with. Trials of thousands found no benefit.

items.note: Children with more lead in their blood score lower on IQ tests.
items.verdict: It damages nerve cells in lab animals, and more lead means lower scores.

source: Der et al., BMJ, 2006; Green et al., JCO, 2011
reference: Der, Batty and Deary, Effect of breast feeding on intelligence in children, BMJ 333:945, 2006; Green et al., Reduced melanoma after regular sunscreen use, J Clin Oncol 29:257-263, 2011; HOPE Study Investigators, Vitamin E supplementation and cardiovascular events, NEJM 342:154-160, 2000; Lei et al., HPV vaccination and the risk of invasive cervical cancer, NEJM 383:1340-1348, 2020
